name: Ovagen

card.summary: Khavinson liver-targeted tripeptide (EDL) with essentially no verifiable published human data and no appearance use.
card.note: Very thin sourcing; not an appearance product.

quick.overview:
Ovagen is a three-amino-acid peptide (Glu-Asp-Leu) developed by Vladimir Khavinson's group in Russia and described as targeting liver and gut tissue.

Verified published studies on it are scarce, and none address appearance.
quick.mechanism: Its developers propose that short peptides bind DNA and regulate gene expression; this has not been confirmed independently.
quick.risks: No human safety data could be verified. It is sold as a research compound or supplement and is not an approved drug in most countries.

lead: Ovagen is a synthetic tripeptide with the sequence Glu-Asp-Leu (EDL), developed by Vladimir Khavinson's group in Russia as part of its Cytogen family of short peptides, according to Grokipedia, an AI-generated encyclopedia.[1] It is sold as a peptide bioregulator for the liver and gastrointestinal tract, and it appears in longevity circles as part of the idea that organ-specific short peptides support tissue upkeep and healthy aging.[1][2]

The appearance link is indirect and claimed: people who follow the Khavinson peptide approach say supporting liver and gut function contributes to general health, which they associate with a healthier look and slower visible aging. No source examined measures skin, hair or body appearance after Ovagen.

Grokipedia states that published evidence is limited to animal models, cell cultures and studies from Russian institutions, and that no large Western randomised trials exist; it is marketed as a research compound or supplement rather than an approved drug.[1] Khavinson (1946-2024) directed the St. Petersburg Institute of Bioregulation and Gerontology, and Wikipedia reports that six of his peptide bioregulators were approved for medical use in the USSR and Russia, with much of the supporting literature coming from his own group.[2]

chain: Short peptide is taken orally or sublingually as a bioregulator
Proposed gene-expression effects in liver and gut tissue
Claimed general health support, linked by followers to healthy aging
angle.text: Followers of the Khavinson peptide approach present Ovagen as a liver and digestive bioregulator that supports general health and aging well. No study found measures appearance outcomes.

infobox: Oral capsules, sublingual drops, research powder[1]

paras: Grokipedia gives the molecular formula as C15H25N3O8 and describes the peptide as chemically synthesised, with proposed DNA binding and effects on chromatin and methylation.[1] These mechanisms are hypotheses from the developing group and the source is not independent.

Khavinson's work on peptide bioregulators began in the 1970s at the S.M. Kirov Military Medical Academy and continued at the St. Petersburg Institute of Bioregulation and Gerontology, founded in 1992, according to Grokipedia.[1] Wikipedia describes bioregulators as peptides of two to four amino acids extracted from animal organs or synthesised, and notes six were approved for medical use in the USSR and Russia, mainly for military medicine.[2] Cytogens, the synthetic series that includes Ovagen, are described as introduced in the early 2000s.[1]

Ovagen is sold as a supplement or research compound rather than as an approved drug in most countries.[1] Wikipedia notes that its own article on Khavinson carries a maintenance notice about promotional content and that much of the supporting material comes from his own publications and institution.[2]
No studies found. Searches for the name Ovagen return veterinary papers on an unrelated purified follicle-stimulating hormone product of the same brand name, which are not studies of the EDL peptide.

timeline.event: St. Petersburg Institute of Bioregulation and Gerontology established.[1]
Cytogen family of synthetic short peptides introduced.[1]
